Stuck in the same shapes and keys?

Most guitarists learn a few open chords, a couple of barre shapes and one scale box — and then stay there. The songs they play, write and arrange end up sounding the same, because their hands always go back to the same spots on the neck and the same few keys.

Guitar Workouts is practice to get out of that box. Every lesson takes one idea — a chord shape, an inversion, a scale position, an arpeggio — and makes you play it in all 12 keys and all over the neck, until you stop thinking about shapes and start hearing music. That is what lets you play any song anywhere, write your own parts and find the sound you hear in your head.

A complete guitar practice path

Six modules that build on each other, from chords to melody. Each lesson has a version for every key.

CAGED system exercises

Basic Chords with CAGED: the five open-chord shapes — C, A, G, E and D — moved up the neck. Major, minor, dominant seventh and half-diminished chords in five regions of the fretboard.

Triad inversion exercises

Triad Inversions: major, minor and diminished triads in root position and with the third or the fifth in the bass, on the 3rd, 4th, 5th and 6th strings — the smallest, most flexible voicings for comping and arranging.

Seventh chord inversion exercises

Seventh Chord Inversions: maj7, m7, 7 and m7(♭5) in root position and with the third, fifth and seventh in the bass, on the 4th, 5th and 6th strings — drop 2 voicings, with drop 3 alternatives.

Major scale exercises in 7 positions

7 Positions of the Ionian Mode: the major scale in seven three-notes-per-string shapes, from the nut to the bridge, plus a warm-up for position shifts.

Triad arpeggio exercises

Triad Arpeggios: major, minor and diminished triads note by note, starting on the root, third or fifth, in three fingerings — then their inversions and the diatonic triads of each key, across the neck and within each scale position.

Seventh chord arpeggio exercises

Seventh Chord Arpeggios: maj7, m7, 7 and m7(♭5) note by note, starting on the root, third, fifth or seventh — then their inversions and the diatonic seventh chords of each key, across the neck and within each scale position.

How a lesson works

  1. 1

    See it

    Chords appear as diagrams with fingers, barres and the degree of every string. Scales and arpeggios appear as fretboard shapes, and melodic exercises as tablature you can switch to standard notation.

  2. 2

    Hear it

    The app plays every chord and every note with a guitar sound, and the note that is sounding lights up, so you can check your hands by ear.

  3. 3

    Play it in time

    Each lesson ends with a run of all its shapes to a metronome. Raise the tempo little by little — the app remembers your last BPM for each lesson.

From practice to music

Play

Know every chord and scale in every key and region of the neck, so you can accompany any song, transpose on the spot and follow other musicians wherever they go.

Compose

Practise the diatonic chords of each key until you hear them, so chord progressions, riffs and melodies come from your ear instead of from the same old shapes.

Arrange

Use inversions and arpeggios to choose the bass note, the top note and the region of the neck — smoother voice leading, parts that fit around a singer and lines that sound like you.

Built for real, everyday practice

Short sessions, real progress

Each exercise takes a few minutes: one key, a handful of shapes, one run with the metronome. One key a day covers a whole lesson in under two weeks.

All 12 keys, not just the easy ones

Every lesson has a variation for each key, in the cycle of fourths. A ring around the lesson fills in as you finish keys — no more avoiding A♭ or F♯.

Tablature and standard notation

Melodic exercises are written as tab, with fingers above and bar lines, or as standard notation with the string for each note. Switch with one tap; a built-in guide explains how to read both.

A chord dictionary and a guide for each module

Look up every voicing from the lessons by key and chord quality, and read the guide that explains the theory behind each module.

Your progress saved to your account

Finished lessons and tempos are saved in your free account and synced across your devices.

Online guitar practice, nothing to install

Everything runs in the browser, on a computer, tablet or phone, in English or Portuguese. The guitar sound is generated live.

Find your own sound on the guitar

Rock, pop, blues, MPB, bossa nova or jazz: freedom on the fretboard is what lets you stop copying shapes and start making choices.

Frequently asked questions

Is it free?

Yes. All lessons, the chord dictionary and the guides are free. You just create a free account to start practicing and save your progress.

Who is it for?

Guitarists who already play a few chords and want to know the whole fretboard: to stop depending on a handful of shapes and keys, and to play, compose and arrange with more freedom. Beginners can start with the CAGED module.

Is it for acoustic or electric guitar?

Both. The shapes are the same on acoustic, classical and electric guitar in standard tuning (E A D G B E).

Do I need to read music?

No. Chords are shown as diagrams and scales as fretboard shapes. Melodic exercises are in tablature by default, and standard notation is optional.

Why practise in all 12 keys?

Because songs, singers and bands use all of them. Practising every shape in every key turns it into a pattern you understand, not a position you memorised, so changing key stops being a problem.

What is the CAGED system?

CAGED maps the guitar neck with the five open-chord shapes C, A, G, E and D. Moving those shapes up the neck lets you play any chord in any key in five regions of the fretboard.

What are chord inversions?

A chord is inverted when a note other than the root is in the bass. A triad has root position and two inversions; a seventh chord has root position and three: third, fifth or seventh in the bass.

What is an arpeggio?

An arpeggio is a chord played one note at a time. Practising arpeggios connects chords and scales: it shows where each chord tone is on the neck, which is the base for soloing over chord changes and for writing melodies.

Does it work on a phone?

Yes. The app works in any modern browser on phones, tablets and computers. Use headphones or a speaker to hear the low strings well.
